articles.headline: Pfizer leaps into 'in vivo' CAR-T with latest China deal
articles.summary: Pfizer has signed a potentially $2.6 billion collaboration with China-based Starna Therapeutics to develop in vivo CAR-T cell therapies targeting autoimmune diseases, joining a competitive race to reprogram immune cells inside the body rather than through costly ex vivo manufacturing. The deal reflects Pfizer's strategic push to build a next-generation cell therapy platform as a growth engine beyond crowded GLP-1 and oncology spaces. It also continues Pfizer's pattern of China-sourced licensing deals as it seeks pipeline replenishment amid post-COVID revenue normalization.
articles.why_it_matters: This deal signals where Big Pharma is placing long-term bets on durable autoimmune moats, with direct read-throughs for competing in vivo cell therapy platforms and potential M&A targets in the space.

articles.headline: Money Stuff: The Agents Will Trade the Bonds
articles.summary: Matt Levine explores the emerging reality of autonomous AI agents trading bonds and other financial instruments, using the concept of MEV (maximal extractable value) from DeFi as a lens to examine how agentic systems will reshape market microstructure, liquidity dynamics, and regulatory accountability in traditional fixed-income markets. He interrogates who bears liability when an AI agent executes a trade gone wrong, and how existing compliance and risk frameworks struggle to accommodate non-human decision-makers operating at machine speed. The piece is characteristically Levine: a specific emerging-tech development used to illuminate deep structural questions about how markets actually work.
articles.why_it_matters: AI agents entering bond markets is a structural shift with direct implications for liquidity provision, compliance infrastructure, and risk management — and understanding this dynamic early is relevant for anyone positioning around market-structure winners or assessing operational risk in financial services.

articles.headline: A Layman Thinks About AI (Howard Marks / Oaktree memo)
articles.summary: Howard Marks applies his signature risk-first, second-level thinking to AI investing, organizing the memo around a series of hard questions: how AI actually works (citing Claude on interpretability gaps), what it will be able to do, who will capture value, and whether current valuations reflect realistic probability-weighted outcomes. He is characteristically skeptical of consensus bullishness, emphasizing the multiplicative uncertainty across technology evolution, competitive structure, demand forecasting, and timing. Rather than offering a buy/sell verdict, he frames AI as a domain where the incompleteness of investor knowledge is unusually high — and argues that acknowledging this is itself a form of edge.
articles.why_it_matters: For a reader who prizes analytical depth and structural market insight, this memo is a rare document: a credible long-term capital allocator stress-testing the AI consensus narrative with a probabilistic framework, directly relevant to portfolio positioning in AI-adjacent equities.
